title: Changing the caller’s variables

prereqs.why: A reference parameter is another name for the caller’s variable, and that is the only way a function can change it.
The difference between a parameter that is a copy and one that is not is the whole exercise.

statement:
Write a function

```cpp
void swapInts(int& a, int& b);
```

that exchanges the values of the two variables the caller passed.
Read two integers, print them, call the function, and print them
again:

```
input:   3 8

output:  before 3 8
         after 8 3
```

### The point of the problem

Write it without the ampersands and nothing happens:

```cpp
void swapInts(int a, int b)        // does nothing useful
{
    int t{ a };
    a = b;
    b = t;
}
```

The function swaps its own two copies and then they are destroyed.
The caller’s variables were never involved. It compiles, it runs,
and `after` prints the same numbers as `before` — which is a
frustrating bug to meet without knowing this rule, because there is
nothing wrong with the swapping code.

An `int&` parameter is **not** a copy. It is another name for the
variable the caller passed, for the duration of the call:

```cpp
void swapInts(int& a, int& b)
{
    int t{ a };
    a = b;
    b = t;
}
```

Nothing changes at the call site. `swapInts(x, y)` looks identical
either way, which is worth knowing: in C++ you cannot tell from a
call whether its arguments can be modified. You have to look at the
declaration.

### Constraints

Both numbers are between -1,000,000 and 1,000,000.

### Boundary cases

- **Two equal values** swap to themselves, which is correct and
  proves nothing — so do not test only with those.
- **Negative values** are no different.
- The three-line swap needs the temporary. `a = b; b = a;`
  overwrites `a` before it has been read, and both variables end up
  holding what `b` held.
hints: The parameters are `int&`, not `int`. Without the ampersands the function swaps two copies and the caller sees nothing.
The body needs a third variable to hold one value while the other is overwritten. Two assignments on their own lose one of them.
Print the two numbers before the call and after it. If both lines are the same, check the parameter types first — the body is probably fine.
